content:
<Rep. Mark Takano>: Ranking Member Takano and Committee Democrats echo the Majority's frustrations with the Department of Veterans Affairs' (VA's) inability to process Adaptive Automobile Equipment (AAE) invoices in a timely manner. Failure to do so puts stress on the businesses providing these necessary adaptations to veterans and risks these businesses leaving the veteran vehicle adaptation space. The Committee must address this issue; however, H.R. 7083 falls short of adequately doing so. Background
AAE claims are fairly unique in VA in that two separate agencies within VA are required to process each claim (the Veterans Health Administration [VHA] and the Veterans Benefits Administration [VBA].) Within VHA, the claims are organized at the Medical Center (VAMC) level ( 170 nationwide), while at VBA they are processed at Regional Offices (ROs, generally one per state with a few in territories/overseas and a couple states having multiple.) To pass claims and information between the agencies, there is not a dedicated IT system. Assigned claims processors scan and email documents back and forth.
At VAMCs, the claims processors can have multiple duties and tend not to stay in the position for long. This means that an employee receiving an AAE claim may need training to properly process it and that claims can easily be lost/delayed because they are emailed to an employee no longer in the position or with the agency. Companies have often expressed frustration due to an inability to reach a point of contact to find out the status of a claim or determine corrections that need to be made.
At ROs, a variety of VA related claims are processed (VA education, Veteran Readiness & Employment, Disability, etc.) AAE claims are a very small portion of the overall number of claims that ROs receive, and AAE claims require specific expertise to process correctly. ROs tend to have a small handful of people trained on AAE claims, but not enough come in for those employees to only work on AAE claims or maintain proficiency. AAE claims are also not tracked in the same systems as the rest of VBA claims. They are received via email from VHA and then must be input into VBA systems for processing/payment. If errors or missing information are identified, the claims processor must come out of the system and email the VHA representative to email the company to send a correction back by email to VHA, who then has to send it back to VBA. It is easy to see how claims can be lost, delayed, or stuck in limbo with so many single points of failure.
Companies that make the AAE adaptations and are attempting to get paid by the VA are often frustrated that the process seems to change depending on which VAMC they are working with. Businesses are also rightly upset that processing times can be ridiculously long because claims packets get lost in the email back and forth or due to employees swapping out, with no one able to track down where the packet is in the process or the issue causing the delay. Addressing the Problems
The VA needs strong leadership from the Department level to direct and oversee the cross-agency collaboration needed to process these claims. The responsible program offices at VHA and VBA need to be held accountable to standardize the process. Positions need to be staffed, and knowledge management processes must be implemented to ensure claims reach completion and issues with individual claims can be remedied.
VBA should be encouraged to centralize processing at several ROs. This is a common practice at VBA for types of claims that require specialization to process correctly or do not have enough volume at individual ROs to keep employees engaged full time. (VBA does this for VA education, Agent Orange, Blue Water Navy, and Military Sexual Trauma claims, to name a few.) Committee Democrats would recommend against reducing it to one RO (as this bill does) as VBA best practices have found that having between 2-5 ROs with specialty teams helps mitigate issues like time zones, weather/facilities closures, and regional specific issues.
VA also needs an IT solution processing these claims. Emailing scanned documents back and forth between agencies only invites delays and failure into this process. Having the claims documents in one database that can be uploaded to/accessed by the claimant, VHA, and VBA would simplify and speed up the process. It would allow proper oversight, standardize the process, identify where claims are stuck, and provide updates to the claimant about timeline for payment. It would also help identify who should be held responsible for failures to process claims in a timely and accurate manner. Shortfalls of the Bill as Written
While Committee Democrats appreciate the Majority taking up the issue, the legislation as written has several shortfalls. The bill directs VA to make payments promptly, but contains no resources to make that happen, no incentives to encourage VA leadership to focus on making it happen, and no penalties to motivate VA to correct itself when it fails to do so. VA is already required to make these payments in a timely manner, but has not prioritized doing so. This legislation does not meaningfully change the status quo.
The Majority's approach to legislating without oversight also falls short. Requiring VA to conduct frequent updates or meet with the Committee would drive faster change in the Department. Holding a hearing or series of hearings on the topic would have forced VA leadership to own the problem and focus on fixing it. The bill does not even create or designate an official to be held accountable for fixing the problem going forward. Attempting to legislate a solution a few months before the end of a Congress realistically means that any solution is likely punted to years in the future.
The legislation also requires no planning for an IT solution or set aside funding for creating one. It is unlikely VA starts planning one under its own volition for a variety of reasons, so Congress failing to direct them to do so means that veterans, companies, and claims processors will be stuck in the status quo of emailing documents back and forth.
Minority Democrats are glad some of the more destructive ideas from the Majority's first drafts were removed, but this version is still lacking. If this bill becomes law as written, this Committee and Congress will likely be trying to address this issue yet again in a future Congress.
Mark Takano,
Ranking Member.
